~3,000 YEARS AGO
How do you carry
water across a desert
for many kilometers without
losing it to the sun?
About three thousand years
ago, engineers in ancient
Persia found an answer,
and it was hidden underground.
They called it the qanat.
Builders dug a well
at the foot of
a hill to reach groundwater.
Then they dug a
tunnel with a gentle
downhill slope from that
well to the fields
below, using a line
of vertical shafts for
air and for hauling out soil.
Gravity did the rest.
Why underground?
Because in the desert,
open water evaporates quickly.
A canal on the
surface would lose much
of its water to
the sun and wind.
In a tunnel,
the water stays cool
and much more of it arrives.
Some qanats are still
in use today,
and Iran's qanats are
listed as a UNESCO
World Heritage Site.
The idea spread widely.
In the Sahara of
Algeria, these tunnels
are called foggaras.
In Oman and the
United Arab Emirates, falaj.
In the Turpan Basin
of western China, karez.
And in Peru,
the Nazca region has
underground channels called
puquios.
Different cultures found
the same solution to
the same problem.
Oases also shaped trade.
The Silk Road was
not a single road
but a network of
routes linked by oasis towns.
Caravans carrying silk,
spices and other goods
moved from one water
source to the next.
Cities such as Dunhuang,
Samarkand and Palmyra grew
rich as stops along the way.
Traditional oasis
communities understood
scarcity well.
Water was usually shared
by strict rules,
often by time.
In some North African
oases, each family's share
was measured by simple
water clocks.
In thirteenth-century
Tozeur, in what is
now Tunisia, the scholar
Ibn Chabbat is credited
with writing detailed rules
for sharing the water.
In the desert,
fairness was a matter
of survival.
There is a quieter danger too.
When irrigation water
evaporates under the desert
sun, the salt stays
behind, and year after
year it builds up
in the soil.
This is called salinization.
That is why drainage
matters as much as
bringing water in.
Tunnels, trade routes and
strict rules: people built
whole worlds around a
few hidden drops.
The full story of
the oasis is on Miya's Lab.
